The SARSA agent was first trained on a 100-day sinusoidal flow profile without biofouling, converging to a stable policy in approximately 50 days with mean Cp of 0.4419. Unlike Q-learning methods commonly used in renewable energy applications, SARSA was chosen because Q-learning tends to diverge when applied with linear function approximation methods. The trained agent was then tested on a year-long case study using Mississippi River discharge data from a USGS station in Baton Rouge, with biofouling effects gradually increasing throughout the simulation. Three control cases were compared: perfect control with complete knowledge of biofouling (Case 1), optimal TSR control without biofouling compensation (Case 2), and the adaptive SARSA controller (Case 3). Results showed that the SARSA method generated 0.92% more energy (approximately 58 kWh) than the optimal TSR controller over the year. The SARSA agent successfully adapted to the changing plant dynamics caused by biofouling, maintaining higher Cp values especially in the latter half of the case study when biofouling effects became more severe. The authors note that future work may include other RL algorithms such as actor-critic methods, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and system-level control for HKT arrays. Deliverable 7.4.3: Report on most promising near-term avenues for adoption of Task 7 findings for the research and industrial community, by connecting to relevant current projects and research activity with other groups The report for Deliverable 7.4.3 as originally submitted is appended (which was originally combined with the report for Deliverable 7.4.1.) The report documents industry outreach through conferences and a January 2025 survey of WEC developers, revealing varied experiences with biofouling—some organizations have extensively studied it and implemented cleaning strokes and antifouling coatings, while others haven't yet had long enough deployments to assess impacts. Several respondents expressed interest in control-based biofouling mitigation strategies, suggesting a pathway for future collaboration. 7 Conclusions Improved Modeling of Marine Growth Impacts The project developed quantitative models linking biofouling characteristics to WEC performance degradation. Using WEC-Sim, researchers simulated the RM3 point absorber under varying degrees of hard biofouling, establishing a drag coefficient model that relates surface roughness to hydrodynamic losses. For a cylinder with fineness ratio L/D in axial flow, the drag coefficient follows a sigmoidal relationship with roughness k/D, allowing prediction of drag forces from measurable biofouling characteristics. Simulations at H=2m and resonant period showed PTO power decreasing by 15% with heavy biofouling (k=0.1m), while peak velocity and displacement each decreased by approximately 10%. For marine hydrokinetic turbines, researchers modeled biofouling's effect on the power coefficient curve using experimental data showing that blade roughness decreases both optimal tip-speed ratio and maximum Cp. A logistic growth model captured time-dependent surface coverage, enabling year-long simulations demonstrating cumulative energy losses for LCOE projections. Quantitative Assessment of Failure and Fault Modes The fault reconnaissance study systematically evaluated failure mechanisms across six major WEC subsystems: generator, power electronic switches, WEC body, mooring lines, O-rings/seals, and PTO.
